rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya rejects taking the clause as an omitted matter or affair because the following sentence itself contains an omission.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: تفسير الأمر والشأن لا يكون بجملة فيها محذوف.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If kāna is complete, mā is its object: God chooses every existent, and nothing occurs except by His permission.
rows.anchor: أي إن الله تعالى يختار كل كائن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “They have no choice” is a new sentence counting God's favor in choosing for them, if they accept and understand.
rows.anchor: لهم الخيرة: جملة مستأنفة معناها: تعديد النعمة عليهم في اختيار الله لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people of Paradise praise God with several formulas; their praise is delight rather than an obligation.
rows.anchor: والتحميد هنالك على سبيل اللذة، لا التكليف.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith says the people of Paradise will be inspired to glorify and sanctify God; no transmitter or grading is supplied here.
rows.anchor: وفي الحديث: «يلهمون التسبيح والتقديس»

rows.speaker: ابن محيصن
rows.claim: Ibn Muḥayṣin reads the verb with an open tāʾ and a damma on the kāf.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن محيصن: ما تكن، بفتح التاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “His is the judgment” means His decree and His deciding between His servants; araytum means “tell me.”
rows.anchor: وله الحكم: أي القضاء بين عباده والفصل.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the competing araytum and jaʿala construction, the second verb governs; omitted complements are recoverable, and the two verbs need not demand the same case role.
rows.anchor: ولا يلزم في باب التنازع أن يستوي المتنازعان في جهة التعدي مطلقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second object of araytum is usually an interrogative clause, unlike jaʿala when it means to create; an object after that sense is circumstantial.
rows.anchor: وكذلك أرأيتم ثاني مفعوليه جملة استفهامية غالبا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some derive sarmadan from sarmad with an added mīm, an irregular form to be learned rather than generated by a rule.
rows.anchor: وسرمدا، قيل: من السرمد، فميمه زائدة، ووزنه فعمل

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī explains the different questions by the benefits of daylight and darkness: hearing suits listed daylight benefits, while sight suits visible rest at night.
rows.anchor: أفلا تبصرون؟ لأن غيرك يبصر من منفعة الظلام ما تبصره أنت من السكون ونحوه، قال الزمخشري.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse says “light” rather than a day for ordinary activity because daylight has many benefits, whereas darkness chiefly offers rest.
rows.anchor: لأن منافع الضياء متكاثرة، ليس التصرف في المعاش وحده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min in “by His mercy” gives the cause; the verse then gives night its purpose, day its purpose, and gratitude as the reason-like conclusion.
rows.anchor: ومن رحمته، من هنا للسبب، أي وبسبب رحمته إياكم، جعل لكم الليل والنهار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This ordering is the rhetorical figure tafsīr: things are named and then explained in fitting sequence, illustrated by Ibn Jayyūs's poem.
rows.anchor: وهذا النوع من علم البديع يسمى التفسير، وهو أن تذكر أشياء ثم تفسرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in fīhi refers to night; in faḍlihi it may refer to God, or metaphorically to daytime because the favor occurs then.
rows.anchor: والضمير في فيه عائد على الليل، وفي فضله يجوز أن يكون عائدا على الله، والتقدير: من فضله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated scene of God calling the idolaters is repeated to communicate and reinforce the warning.
rows.anchor: تقدم الكلام على قوله: ويوم يناديهم: وكرر هنا على جهة الإبلاغ والتأكيد.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nazaʿnā means swiftly separating and drawing out; the witness is each community's prophet, who testifies that the message was delivered.
rows.anchor: ونزعنا: أي ميزنا وأخرجنا بسرعة من كل أمة من الأمم. شهيدا: وهو نبي تلك الأمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view takes shahīd collectively as the just and excellent people of each community.
rows.anchor: وقيل: عدولا وخيارا. والشهيد على هذا اسم الجنس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The community is asked to produce its proof for opposing the witness and rejecting monotheism; they then recognize that truth belongs to God, not their idols.
rows.anchor: هاتوا برهانكم: أي حجتكم فيما كنتم عليه في الدنيا من الكفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What they fabricated disappears from them as a lost thing.
rows.anchor: وضل عنهم: أي وغاب عنهم غيبة الشيء الضائع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qārūn is a foreign proper name and is indeclinable for foreignness and proper-name status; “from his people” may mean one who believed in Moses.
rows.anchor: وقارون أعجمي: منع الصرف للعجمة والعلمية

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya says Qārūn was an Israelite by consensus.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: وهو إسرائيلي بإجماع.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Among conflicting genealogies, the strongest is Ibn ʿAbbās's report that Qārūn was Moses's cousin, son of Yishhar, son of Qāhith.
rows.anchor: وأولاها: ما قاله ابن عباس أنه ابن عمه، وهو قارون ابن يصهر بن قاهث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qārūn was called al-Munawwar for his handsome appearance, knew and recited the Torah best among the Israelites, then became a hypocrite like al-Sāmirī.
rows.anchor: وكان يسمى المنور لحسن صورته، وكان أحفظ بني إسرائيل للتوراة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His transgressions included unbelief, arrogance, envy of Moses's prophethood and Aaron's sacrificial role, oppression under Pharaoh, and arranging a woman's false accusation against Moses.
rows.anchor: فبغى عليهم: ذكروا من أنواع بغيه الكفر والكبر، وحسده لموسى على النبوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reported sign of his arrogance was adding a handspan to his clothes.
rows.anchor: ومن تكبره أن زاد في ثيابه شبرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view says God gave him a treasure of Joseph; another says his wealth was called treasure because he withheld its zakāt, beginning his hostility toward Moses.
rows.anchor: آتيناه من الكنوز، قيل: أظفره الله بكنز من كنوز يوسف عليه السلام.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relative mā is connected to inna and its complements; al-Naḥḥās cites al-Akhfash against the Kūfan restriction on such relative clauses.
rows.anchor: وما موصولة، صلتها إن ومعمولاها.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The keys are variously glossed as treasury keys, the treasuries themselves, or their containers; al-Aʿmash reads “his keys.”
rows.anchor: وقالوا هنا: مقاليد خزائنه. وقال السدي: هي الخزائن نفسها. وقال الضحاك: ظروفه وأوعيته.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports of the number of keys were so extravagant that the author omits them as lies or near-lies.
rows.anchor: وذكروا من كثرة مفاتحه ما هو كذب، أو يقارب الكذب، فلم أكتبه.

rows.speaker: أبو زيد
rows.claim: Abū Zayd defines nāʾa bi-l-ʿamal as rising while bearing it; cited poetry illustrates the verb's sense of bearing a heavy load.
rows.anchor:
قال أبو زيد:
نؤت بالعمل إذا نهضت به.

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda treats the syntax as inversion: the keys weigh down the group, as though the text said the group bears them.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: هو مقلوب وأصله: لتنوء بها العصبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bāʾ is causative: the keys make the group heavy, a construction also attributed to al-Khalīl, Sībawayh, al-Farrāʾ, and preferred by al-Naḥḥās.
rows.anchor: والصحيح أن الباء للتعدية، أي لتنيء العصبة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The causative sense is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū Ṣāliḥ, and al-Suddī; Arabs say a load weighs down a camel.
rows.anchor: وروي معناه عن ابن عباس وأبي صالح والسدي، وتقول العرب: ناء الحمل بالبعير

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya allows the keys to be the grammatical subject: they rise with effort when the carrier lifts them.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: ويمكن أن يسند تنوء إلى المفاتح

rows.speaker: بديل بن ميسرة
rows.claim: Budayl reads the verb in masculine singular, explained by an omitted masculine noun such as the load of the keys; al-Zamakhsharī offers a related attachment explanation.
rows.anchor: وقرأ بديل بن ميسرة: لينوء، بالياء، وتذكيره راعى المضاف المحذوف

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو الداني
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī reports Budayl's singular “key,” which removes the need to explain the masculine verb.
rows.anchor: وذكر أبو عمرو الداني إن بديل بن ميسرة قرأ: ما إن مفتاحه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan are also cited for taking the keys to mean the wealth itself.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس والحسن: أن المفاتح هي الأموال.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that forty strong men carried Qārūn's treasuries, said here to number four hundred thousand, ten thousand per carrier.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: كانت خزائنه تحملها أربعون أقوياء، وكانت أربعمائة ألف

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim takes the keys as knowledge and exhaustive awareness, like God's “keys of the unseen”; guarding so many kinds of treasure burdens its keepers.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو مسلم: المراد من المفاتح: العلم والإحاطة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qārūn's people condemn the arrogant, intoxicating joy of someone absorbed in worldly success and heedless of the afterlife.
rows.anchor: إذ قال له قومه لا تفرح: نهوه عن الفرح المطغي الذي هو انهماك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū al-Ṭayyib's verse illustrates that joy in a passing fortune is grief because its owner knows it will depart.
rows.anchor:
وقال أبو الطيب:
أشد الغم عندي في سرور

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī makes id dependent on the burdening of the keys; the author rejects this because that burden is not confined to the time of the rebuke.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: ومحل إذ منصوب بتنوء. انتهى، وهذا ضعيف جدا

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya links id to Qārūn's transgression, while al-Ḥawfī and Abū al-Baqāʾ propose other links; the author finds these timing connections weak.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: متعلق بقوله: فبغى عليهم، وهو ضعيف أيضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author supplies an omitted act of showing off: Qārūn displayed pride in his treasures when his people told him not to rejoice.
rows.anchor: ويظهر أن يكون تقديره: فأظهر التفاخر والفرح بما أوتي من الكنوز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning against rejoicing recalls 57:23; an Arab poem praises not exulting when fortune smiles or despairing when it turns.
rows.anchor: وقال تعالى: ولا تفرحوا بما آتاكم ، والعرب تمدح بترك الفرح

rows.speaker: عيسى بن سليمان الحجازي
rows.claim: ʿĪsā ibn Sulaymān al-Ḥijāzī reports the reading al-fāriḥīn.
rows.anchor: وقرىء: الفارحين، حكاه عيسى بن سليمان الحجازي.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “God does not love” describes an act, not an attribute of essence: here it means He does not extend blessing and mercy to the arrogant.
rows.anchor: ولا يحب: صفة فعل، لا صفة ذات، بمعنى الإرادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After warning against arrogant joy, the people tell Qārūn to use God's wealth for afterlife reward through good works.
rows.anchor: أمروه بأن يطلب، فيما آتاه الله من الكنوز وسعة الرزق، ثواب الدار الآخرة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and most commentators say not to neglect one's share of worldly life means not wasting one's lifetime without good deeds, since the afterlife is earned here.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس، والجمهور: معناه: ولا تضيع عمرك في أن لا تعمل صالحا

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and Qatāda instead understand the phrase as permitting lawful enjoyment, seeking it, and prudent attention to worldly needs.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن، وقتادة: معناه: لا تضيع حظك من الدنيا في تمتعك بالحلال

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan also says to give away the surplus while retaining enough to live on.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: معناه: قدم الفضل وأمسك ما تبلغ به.

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Mālik glosses one's share as eating and drinking without extravagance.
rows.anchor: وقال مالك: هو الأكل والشرب بلا سرف.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another admonition says that one's only worldly share of amassed wealth may be a shroud and burial spices, illustrated by a poem.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أرادوا بنصيبه الكفن، وهذا وعظ متصل

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says to take from worldly life what suffices and benefits you, close to al-Ḥasan's interpretation.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: أن تأخذ منه ما يكفيك ويصلحك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Do good as God did good to you” can use the kāf for comparison in a limited respect, or for causation: do good because God favored you.
rows.anchor: والكاف للتشبيه، وهو يكون في بعض الأوصاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Do not seek corruption” rebukes Qārūn for the oppression he was already committing.
rows.anchor: ولا تبغ الفساد: أي ما أنت عليه من البغي والظلم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word ʿilm is a verbal noun that may be construed as knowledge belonging to Qārūn or as knowledge from God.
rows.anchor: على علم، علم: مصدر، يحتمل أن يكون مضافا إليه ومضافا إلى الله.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most commentators say Qārūn claimed his knowledge entitled him to the treasures; one view identifies it with Torah learning and selection among Moses's seventy delegates, but calls that sophistry.
rows.anchor: فقال الجمهور: ادعى أن عنده علما استوجب به أن يكون صاحب تلك الكنوز.

rows.speaker: أبو سليمان الداني
rows.claim: Abū Sulaymān al-Dānī takes the claimed knowledge as commerce and methods of earning: Qārūn says his own intelligence and effort gained the wealth.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو سليمان الداني: أي علم التجارة ووجوه المكاسب

rows.speaker: ابن المسيب
rows.claim: Ibn al-Musayyib identifies the knowledge as alchemy; a report says Moses knew it as transmuting lead and copper into gold.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن المسيب: علم الكيمياء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Alchemy is also attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās as knowledge of the craft, but the author doubts these attributions and cites al-Zajjāj's denial of alchemy.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس: على علم الصنعة الذهب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author criticizes Egyptian seekers of alchemy and similar impossibilities, noting that even their religious elders solicit such claims from ignorant visitors.
rows.anchor: وكثيرا ما تولع أهل مصر بطلب أشياء من المستحيلات والخرافات

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd and others say Qārūn claimed God had specially selected him for the wealth, so he owed nothing to his critics.
rows.anchor:
وقال ابن زيد وغيره: أراد:
أوتيته على علم من الله وتخصيص من لدنه قصدني به

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil glosses the claim as wealth given on account of good that God knew Qārūn possessed.
rows.anchor:
وقال مقاتل:
على علم، أي على خير علمه الله عندي.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Did he not know?” reminds Qārūn that stronger and richer earlier peoples were destroyed; he could know this from Torah, Moses, or histories and should not trust his wealth.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن قوله: أولم يعلم، تقرير لعلمه ذلك، وتنبيه على خطئه في اغتراره

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī asks whether Qārūn possessed this useful knowledge of how to avoid the fate of those destroyed, despite boasting of knowledge.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: ويجوز أن يكون نعتا لعلمه بذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Greater in gathering” may mean greater wealth or more people to protect and serve; Ibn ʿAtiyya says the wording reinforces Qārūn's self-conceit.
rows.anchor: وأكثر جمعا، إما للمال، أو جماعة يحوطونه ويخدمونه.

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب
rows.claim: Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb connects the passive “they are not asked about their sins” to the preceding destruction: God did not need to ask the destroyed peoples.
rows.anchor: قاله محمد بن كعب. والضمير في ذنوبهم عائد على من أهلك من القرون

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says the destroyed are not asked because God already knows their sins; elsewhere he says the guilty's sins are obvious and they enter Hell without reckoning.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: لا يسألون عن ذنوبهم لظهورها وكثرتها

rows.speaker: جابر
rows.claim: Jābir and Mujāhid are cited for Qārūn wearing red clothes; other reports describe his retinue in dyed, purple, or silk finery and extravagant numbers.
rows.anchor: قال جابر، مجاهد: في ثياب حمر.

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar reads the phrase as a prohibition addressed to the Prophet, with “the guilty” in the accusative; Ibn Sīrīn and Abū al-ʿĀliya likewise read the prohibition.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو جعفر في روايته: ولا تسأل، بالتاء والجزم، المجرمين: نصب.

rows.speaker: ابن أبي إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Abī Isḥāq allows the prohibitive reading only if al-mujrimīn is accusative as the verb's object; the author discusses alternatives if it remains nominative.
rows.anchor: وكان ابن أبي إسحاق لا يجوز ذلك إلا إن يكون المجرمين بالياء في محل النصب

rows.speaker: صاحب اللوامح
rows.claim: The author of al-Lawāmiḥ offers a nominative analysis by supplying a subject or treating the noun as a return to the underlying case of the pronoun; the author says the analogous reading lacks evidence.
rows.anchor: قال صاحب اللوامح: فالظاهر ما قاله، ولم يبلغني في نصب المجرمين شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qatāda and Mujāhid say angels recognize sinners from their dark, disfigured signs, as in 55:41; another view says this is not a question of reproach.
rows.anchor: لا تسألهم الملائكة عن ذنوبهم، لأنهم يعرفونهم بسيماهم من السواد والتشويه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After describing Qārūn's wealth and arrogant claim, the passage shows him displaying the finest clothing, mounts, and worldly adornment to his people on Saturday.
rows.anchor: ولما ذكر تعالى قارون ونعته، وما آتاه من الكنوز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who coveted Qārūn's display are variously said to be believers wishing to draw near God, people desiring wealth, or unbelievers; their wish is envy without wanting his loss.
rows.anchor: قال الذين يريدون الحياة الدنيا قيل: كانوا مؤمنين.

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk glosses Qārūn's great ḥaẓẓ as a high rank; another view means a large worldly share, since the word can mean fortune or luck.
rows.anchor: إنه لذو حظ عظيم: أي درجة عظيمة، قاله الضحاك.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those given knowledge include Joshua; their knowledge is variously described as knowing reward and punishment, reliance on God, or foreknowledge.
rows.anchor: وقال الذين أوتوا العلم، منهم: يوشع، والعلم: معرفة الثواب والعقاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's afterlife reward is better than Qārūn's wealth; “none receives it” can mean the wisdom, Paradise and its delights, or the statement itself, and only the patient attain it.
rows.anchor: ولا يلقاها: أي هذه الحكمة، وهي معرفة ثواب الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A long account says Qārūn paid a woman to accuse Moses, she repented and exposed him, and the earth swallowed Qārūn and his followers; the author says God knows that story best.
rows.anchor: فأمر الله الأرض أن تطيعه، فقال: يا أرض خذيه وأتباعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min in “no faction” comprehensively negates every group that could aid Qārūn; lacking a group makes the failure of any individual to help even clearer, and he could not resist God himself.
rows.anchor: ومن زائدة، أي من جماعة تفيد استغراق الفئات

none: Qurʾanic verses 29:45–64 are quoted without commentary in this segment.

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report says the Messenger called Mihja the chief of martyrs and the first summoned to the gate of Paradise; the passage also mentions Ayyāsh, who was deceived and apostatized.
rows.anchor: وقال فيه رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: «سيد الشهداء مهجع وهو أول من يدعى إلى باب الجنة»

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan identifies “the people” as hypocrites who expect to be left alone merely for saying “we believe.”
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: الناس هنا المنافقون، أي أن يتركوا لمجرد قولهم آمنا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb ḥasiba takes two objects; several grammarians parse the clause after it as filling both, or as a substitute or an object after an omitted preposition.
rows.anchor: وحسب يطلب مفعولين. فقال الحوفي، وابن عطية، وأبو البقاء

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī parses “being left untested for saying we believe” as the two objects, with the untested phrase completing the sense of leaving someone in a state.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: فإن قلت: فأين الكلام الدال على المضمون

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya distinguishes the prepositions: bāʾ suggests leaving someone in a state, while lām means “because of”; the author later finds al-Zamakhsharī's account inconsistent.
rows.anchor:
قال ابن عطية:
والمعنى في الباء واللام مختلف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects al-Zamakhsharī's claim that leaving here means transforming: “untested” is a circumstantial phrase, not the required second object of a transformative verb.
rows.anchor: وهذا لا يصح، لأن مفعول صير الثاني لا يستقيم أن يكون لقولهم

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Shaʿbī says the believers' test was being required to emigrate, from which they were not excused.
rows.anchor: قال الشعبي: الفتنة هنا ما كلفه المؤمنون من الهجرة

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī gives another gloss for the test, citing the threat of being divided into factions.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: هو مثال، أو يلبسكم شيعا

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says the test reaches believers' own persons and their property.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: يتبتلون في أنفسهم وأموالهم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earlier believers endured ordeals such as being sawn apart or combed with iron without abandoning their faith; God's testing distinguishes truthful faith from false claims.
rows.anchor: والذين من قبلهم: المؤمنون أتباع الأنبياء، أصابهم من المحن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's “knowing” cannot mean acquiring new knowledge; it means distinguishing the truthful from liars, or manifesting His already eternal knowledge in the event.
rows.anchor: والمعنى: وليميزن الصادق منهم من الكاذب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Truthfulness in faith means that deeds agree with one's profession and belief; liars are the opposite.
rows.anchor: ومعنى صدقوا في أيمانهم يطابق قولهم واعتقادهم أفعالهم

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: ʿAlī and Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad read the verb in a causative form; the omitted object may be their stations in the afterlife or the people whom God makes recognize them.
rows.anchor: وقرأ علي، وجعفر بن محمد: فليعلمن

rows.speaker: الزهري
rows.claim: Al-Zuhrī reads the first occurrence like the majority and the second like ʿAlī's reading.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الزهري: الأولى كقراءة الجماعة، والثانية كقراءة علي.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects Ibn ʿAtiyya's treating am as paired with the opening question: a connected am needs a single item or alternatives, while this clause shifts to a new rebuking question, “rather.”
rows.anchor: وليست أم هنا معادلة للألف في أحسب، كما ذكر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the evil-doers first addressed as leading Quraysh, including al-Walīd, Abū Jahl, al-Aswad, and ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil; the verse applies generally to every sinner.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد الوليد بن المغيرة، وأبا جهل، والأسود

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid glosses the evil-doers' hope of outstripping God as thinking they can escape Him; other glosses are evading or hastening the decree.
rows.anchor: أن يسبقونا: أي يعجزونا، فلا نقدر على الانتقام

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says sinners act as if they expect to escape because of heedlessness, although the punishment will inevitably catch them.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: أن يسبقونا: أن يفوتونا، يعني أن الجزاء يلحقهم لا محالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author objects that these Quraysh leaders believed there was no resurrection or judgment, so al-Zamakhsharī's account wrongly treats them as expecting a possible pardon.
rows.anchor: بل هم معتقدون أن لا بعث ولا جزاء

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says the clause after an fills the two objects of ḥasiba; he also allows ḥasiba to mean “estimate,” a nonstandard implication the author says is unnecessary.
rows.anchor: اشتمال صلة أن على مسند ومسند إليه سد مسد المفعولين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mā in “evil is what they judge” may be a relative pronoun, an accusative of specification, or a verbal noun; the present tense either marks continuing blame or serves rhyme.
rows.anchor: وفي كون ما موصولة مرفوعة بساء، أو منصوبة على التمييز خلاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hoping to meet God means reaching the outcome of death, resurrection, and recompense, compared to a servant returning from a journey to his master.
rows.anchor: ومعنى لقاء الله: الوصول إلى عاقبة الأمر من الموت والبعث والجزاء

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda glosses yarjū as “fears”; the author favors its apparent sense of hoping and supplies an implied command to do good.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: يرجو: يخاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's appointed meeting will certainly arrive, so a person should hasten righteous work that fulfills his hope.
rows.anchor: فليبادر بالعمل الصالح الذي يحقق رجاءه، فإن ما أجله الله تعالى من لقاء جزائه لآت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Striving means patiently disciplining oneself in obedience; its reward benefits the servant, since God needs neither that person nor creation.
rows.anchor: ومن جاهد نفسه بالصبر على الطاعات، فثمرة جهاده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Forgiving sins includes a convert's pre-Islamic sins and a believer's later misdeeds, which may be outweighed by good deeds; the best reward means the best recompense, tenfold.
rows.anchor: لنكفرن عنهم سيئاتهم: يشمل من كان كافرا فآمن وعمل صالحا

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya supplies “reward of” before “the best of what they did”; the author says this wrongly leaves the reward for ordinary good deeds unmentioned.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: فيه حذف مضاف تقديره: ثواب أحسن الذي كانوا يعملون.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage urges those who stayed behind from emigration to make up their lapse and praises believers who emigrated promptly.
rows.anchor: وفي هذه الآيات تحريك وهزا لمن تخلف عن الجهرة

rows.speaker: الترمذي
rows.claim: Al-Tirmidhī reports the verse was revealed about Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, whose mother swore not to eat or drink until he renounced Islam.
rows.anchor: في جامع الترمذي: إنها نزلت في سعد بن أبي وقاص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another occasion report concerns ʿAyyāsh ibn Abī Rabīʿa: his mother swore similarly, and Abū Jahl and his brother tricked, bound, beat, and returned him to her.
rows.anchor: وقيل: في عياش بن أبي ربيعة، أسلم وهاجر مع عمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥusnan can be an adjective of the omitted verbal noun, meaning a good charge to care for parents; Ibn ʿAtiyya offers other syntactic analyses, continued in the next segment.
rows.anchor: وانتصب حسنا على أنه مصدر، وصف به مصدر وصينا

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya allows ḥusnan as an object or as an emphatic verbal noun; cited poetry uses the same construction for urging good treatment.
rows.anchor:
قال ابن عطية:
ويحتمل أن يكون المفعول الثاني في قوله: بوالديه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other analyses supply “good” after the preposition, treat ḥusnan as a cut-off object, or elide “that he do good”; the author objects that some require impermissibly retaining an object's complement after deleting its verb.
rows.anchor: وفي التحرير: حسنا نصب عند البصريين على التكرير

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī reads the phrase as providing good to one's parents, or as an omitted imperative to treat them well; the author objects to some of the assumed deletions.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: وصيناه بإيتاء والديه حسنا

rows.speaker: أبو الفضل الرازي
rows.claim: Abū al-Faḍl al-Rāzī says ḥusnan stands for an omitted noun, “a good matter,” because the preceding verb has already taken its objects.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو الفضل الرازي: وانتصابه بفعل دون التوصية المقدمة

rows.speaker: عيسى
rows.claim: ʿĪsā and al-Jaḥdarī read ḥasanan with two fatḥas; the majority reads ḥusnan with a ḍamma and sukūn, and Ubayy's codex has iḥsānan.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عيسى، والجحدري: حسنا، بفتحتين والجمهور: بضم الحاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If parents press someone to associate a deity with God, they are not to be obeyed; denying knowledge means the supposed deity is not truly divine.
rows.anchor: فلا تطعهما فيما جاهداك عليه من الإشراك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Everyone returns to God, who will report and repay their deeds; the promise of joining the righteous is repeated to spur believers toward that honored rank.
rows.anchor: إلي مرجعكم: شامل للموصي والموصى والمجاهد والمجاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The righteous may mean the company of the righteous or their reward, Paradise; Abraham sought this rank, Solomon asked for it, and God promises it to the obedient.
rows.anchor: ومعنى في الصالحين: في جملتهم، ومرتبة الصلاح شريفة

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says the passage concerns hypocrites who professed faith but let unbelievers' persecution turn them away.
rows.anchor: وكونها نزلت في منافقين، قول ابن زيد.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj, Mujāhid, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk explain that such people panic at human persecution just as they would at God's punishment; Qatāda says some emigrants were returned to Mecca.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: جزع كما يجزع من عذاب الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another report says the verse concerns believers driven out toward Badr who apostatized, the people referenced in 4:97.
rows.anchor: وقيل: في مؤمنين أخرجهم إلى بدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The persecuted claim that they will join the believers if victory comes, hoping to share the spoils; their claim exposes their deceit, since genuine faith would endure persecution.
rows.anchor: وهذه الجملة المقسم عليها مظهرة مغالطتهم، إذ لو كان إيمانهم صحيحا

rows.speaker: أبو معاذ النحوي
rows.claim: Abū Muʿādh al-Naḥwī and al-Zamakhsharī report a reading with fatḥa on the lām of “they will surely say.”
rows.anchor: وقرىء: ليقولن، بفتح اللام، ذكره أبو معاذ النحوي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God knows what lies within believers and hypocrites; the statement about knowing the hypocrites confirms that the preceding discussion concerns them and warns them of punishment.
rows.anchor: وليعلمن المنافقين: ظاهر في أن ما قبل هذه الجملة في المنافقين

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says Quraysh leaders told believers that neither group would be resurrected, but if judgment came they would bear the believers' sins.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: كانوا يقولن لمن آمن منهم: لا نبعث نحن ولا أنتم

rows.speaker: أبو سفيان بن حرب
rows.claim: Another report attributes the promise to Abū Sufyān and Umayya ibn Khalaf speaking to ʿImrān.
rows.anchor: وقيل: قائل ذلك أبو سفيان بن حرب وأمية بن خلف، قال لعمران:

rows.speaker: الوليد بن المغيرة
rows.claim: Another view names al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra as the speaker who promised to bear the believers' sins.
rows.anchor: وقيل: قائل ذلك الوليد بن المغيرة.

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya treats “we will carry” as a report phrased like a command for emphasis; the accompanying poem illustrates that form.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: وقوله: ولنحمل، أخبر أنهم يحملون خطاياهم على جهة التشبيه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī reads the leaders as commanding the believers to follow their way and commanding themselves to bear their sins; the author rejects his phrase “if perhaps it was.”
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: أمروهم باتباع سبيلهم، وهي طريقتهم التي كانوا عليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says al-Zamakhsharī's “if perhaps it was” is ungrammatical Arabic: conditional in is not followed by the frozen verb ʿasā, which also cannot take kāna this way.
rows.anchor: وقوله: فإن عسى، كان تركيب أعجمي لا عربي

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan, ʿĪsā, and Nūḥ read the lām of command with kasra; the reading is also transmitted from ʿAlī.
rows.anchor:
وقرأ الحسن، وعيسى، ونوح القارئ:
ولنحمل، بكسر لام الأمر

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says ḥaml here is a guarantee or surety, not literal carrying; the majority reads “their sins,” while several variants are reported for the singular and plural forms.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: نحمل هنا من الحمالة، لا من الحمل.

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī explains the leaders are called liars because God knows they cannot fulfill their guarantee, or because their hearts contradict their words; Ibn ʿAtiyya also sees their promise as false.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: فإن قلت: كيف سماهم كاذبين؟ وإنما ضمنوا شيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The leaders carry their own burdens of unbelief and sins, plus burdens of those they led astray; a hadith describes the sinner's good deeds being transferred to the wronged.
rows.anchor: وليحملن أثقالهم: أثقال أنفسهم من كفرهم ومعاصيهم، وأثقالا أي أخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith says a wrongdoer may pay the wronged with good deeds, and, if these run out, take on the wronged person's sins.
rows.anchor: كما جاء في الحديث: «أنه يقتص من الظالم للمظلوم بأن يعطى من حسنات ظالمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim reports that anyone who calls to misguidance bears the sins of those who follow and act on it, without reducing their own burden.
rows.anchor: وفي صحيح مسلم ما معناه: أيما داع دعا إلى ضلالة، فاتبع عليها وعمل بها بعده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They will be questioned on Judgment Day in rebuke and reproach.
rows.anchor: وليسئلن يوم القيامة: أي سؤال توبيخ وتقريع.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah's story consoles the Prophet by recalling how the earliest messenger endured his people's harm for a very long time.
rows.anchor: ذكر هذه القصة تسلية لرسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم، لما كان يلقى من أذى الكفار.

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya considers wa-laqad an oath with the sworn subject omitted; the author calls this unlikely because it leaves the preposition without its governed noun.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: والقسم فيها بعيد، يعني أن يكون المقسم به قد حذف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent sense is that Noah spent the stated period among his people calling them to God; Ibn ʿAtiyya's alternative that it covers his entire life is rejected because the following fa marks sequence.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه أقام في قومه هذه المدة المذكورة يدعوهم إلى الله.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception from one thousand supports numerical exception, disputed in Arabic grammar but used by jurists; differing units avoid repetition and the full thousand heightens the long wait, while fifty removes any impression of exaggeration.
rows.anchor: والاستثناء من الألف استدل به على جواز الاستثناء من العدد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “We made it a sign” may refer to the ark or the event; the sign was God's rescue of its passengers and the ark's survival for later people to see.
rows.anchor: والضمير في وجعلناها يحتمل أن يعود على السفينة، وأن يعود على الحادثة والقصة

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya and al-Zamakhsharī parse Ibrāhīm through coordination or an implied “remember”; the author objects that a past-time id is not a direct object here.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: أو على الضمير في فأنجيناه.

rows.speaker: النخعي
rows.claim: Al-Nakhaʿī, Abū Jaʿfar, Abū Ḥanīfa, and Ibrāhīm read the name in the nominative: “and among the messengers was Abraham.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ النخعي، وأبو جعفر، وأبو حنيفة، وإبراهيم: بالرفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's story parallels Quraysh's situation and recalls their forefather's rejection of idols; Nimrod and his city worshipped idols.
rows.anchor: وهذه القصة تمثيل لقريش، وتذكير لحال أبيهم إبراهيم من رفض الأصنام

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Readings differ on tukhliquna and afkan; Ibn ʿAbbās says making idols is called falsehood because their makers falsely claim they are gods.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: وتخلقون إفكا، هو نحت الأصنام وخلقها

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid takes “fabricating falsehood” as inventing lies about idols and other matters; al-Zamakhsharī gives alternative grammatical analyses of afkan.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: هو اختلاف الكذب في أمر الأوثان وغير ذلك.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse argues that idols cannot provide sustenance, whether rizq means the act of provision or the provision itself; God owns all sustenance, so people should seek it from Him and give thanks.
rows.anchor: فقرر أن الأصنام لا ترزق، والرزق يحتمل أن يريد به المصدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Denying the message is no innovation: earlier peoples also denied messengers; one report says Idrīs lived a thousand years, with a thousand believing and the rest rejecting him.
rows.anchor: وإن تكذبوا: أي ليس هذا مبتكرا منكم، وقد سبق ذلك من أمم الرسل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readings vary between direct address and third person in “do they not see,” and between the forms yabdaʾu and yubdiʾu; al-Zuhrī has an unusual eased hamza.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة، والكسائي، وأبو بكر، بخلاف عنه: تروا، بتاء الخطاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What people can observe as the beginning of creation is life returning to earth and bringing things from nonexistence into existence; resurrection and the next creation are separate divine reports, not part of what they see.
rows.anchor: إنما هو لمشاهدتهم إحياء الأرض بالنبات، وإخراج أشياء من العدم إلى الوجود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The visible beginning shows that resurrection is possible; once God's truthful report promises it, its occurrence is certain.
rows.anchor: فإذا أمكن ذلك وأخبر الصادق بوقوعه، صار واجبا مقطوعا بعلمه

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda interprets “do they not see?” as reasoning from proofs that God can restore bodies after death.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: أولم يروا، بالدلائل والنظر كيف يجوز أن يعيد الله الأجسام

rows.speaker: الربيع بن أنس
rows.claim: Al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas says the verse describes human creation beginning and then passing through later states, finally becoming dust.
rows.anchor: وقال الربيع بن أنس المعنى: كيف يبدأ خلق الإنسان ثم يعيده إلى أحوال أخر

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil takes “creation” in this passage to mean night and day.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: الخلق هنا الليل والنهار.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr read al-nashāʾah, while the majority reads al-nashʾah; both are dialect forms and the shortened form is more common.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير، وأبو عمرو: النشاءة هنا، وفي النجم والواقعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage alternates explicit and implicit mention of God's name so each paired sentence names Him; explicit mention in the second pair magnifies the disputed final creation, following creation from nothing with resurrection.
rows.anchor: حتى لا تخلو الجملتان من صريح اسمه. ودل إبرازه هنا على تفخيم النشأة الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God mentions punishment before mercy because the audience is unbelievers denying the messengers; yuqallabūn means they are returned to Him.
rows.anchor: وبدأ بالعذاب، لأن الكلام هو مع الكفار مكذبي الرسل.

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī explains the objects of God's willing as stated elsewhere in the Qur'an, in a way the author labels the Muʿtazilite method.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: ومتعلق المشيئتين مفسر مبين في مواضع من القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People cannot escape God's will; “in the sky” may mean high places such as towers, or the canopy of heaven with an implied “even if you went there,” illustrated by al-Aʿshā's poem.
rows.anchor: في الأرض ولا في السماء، إن حمل السماء على العلو فجائز
